title: Food Photography Tips: Angles, Light and Phone Settings — cv.cm
description: Food photography tips for phones and cameras: overhead, 45 degree or eye-level angles, window side light, props, steam, and restaurant white balance without flash.
h1: How do you take good food photos?
answer: Put the dish near a window so daylight comes from the side or slightly behind, never from the camera's direction. Shoot flat food from directly above, most plates from about 45 degrees, and tall food such as burgers or drinks from the side. Turn off the flash, tap to focus on the most appetizing part, and keep the background simple.

sections.h: Why light direction matters for food
body: Food looks good when you can see its texture: the crust on bread, the gloss on a sauce, the bubbles in a drink. Texture comes from small shadows and highlights, and those only appear when light comes from the side or from behind the food.

Light from the front, such as a phone flash or a lamp behind the photographer, fills every shadow and makes food look flat and greasy. Light from directly above, like most restaurant ceiling lights, puts a hard shadow under the plate and a glare on cutlery. Moving the plate, or yourself, so the light comes from the side is the single biggest improvement you can make.

body: If you are not sure, take one frame from each angle and compare them on the screen. A wide-angle lens very close to food makes the near edge of the plate look huge, so step back and use 2x on a phone, or a 50 mm or longer lens on a camera.

ol: Choose a window without direct sun, or cover it with a thin white curtain or baking paper to soften the sun.
Put the table next to the window so the light comes from the left or right of the dish. For glossy food and drinks, move the dish so the light comes from behind and slightly to the side.
Turn off room lights. Mixing yellow bulbs with daylight gives two colors of light on one plate.
Hold a white card, a sheet of paper or a white napkin on the side away from the window to lighten the shadows. Use a black card instead if you want deeper, moodier shadows.
Place the camera or phone. Use a tripod or rest your elbows on the table so you can keep the same frame while you adjust the food.
Take a test shot, then fix the styling and the light, not just the settings.

body: Camera settings for this setup: aperture priority, f/2.8 to f/4 at 45 degrees, f/5.6 to f/8 overhead, ISO 100 to 400. Handheld, keep the shutter at 1/125 s or faster; on a tripod you can go down to 1/15 s for still food. White dishes and tablecloths fool the meter into underexposing, so add about +0.3 to +1 EV if the plate looks grey.

ul: Pick a plain surface: a wooden board, a stone tile, a linen cloth, or a sheet of matte card. Matte surfaces reflect less glare than glossy ones.
Use plates that are smaller than you think and plain in color. The food should fill most of the plate.
Add one or two props that tell the story: the chopsticks or fork, a napkin, a raw ingredient, a cup of tea. Keep them partly out of frame.
Use odd numbers of small items (three dumplings, five strawberries) and leave some empty space.
Wipe drips from the plate rim with a paper towel or a cotton swab before shooting.
Add fresh herbs, a sprinkle of sesame or a drizzle of sauce at the last moment so they look fresh.
Brush a little oil or water on vegetables and meat that look dry.
Show human touch: a hand holding a spoon, chopsticks lifting noodles, a pour from a jug. Use 1/500 s or faster to freeze the motion.

body: Steam is hard to photograph. It only shows against a dark background with light from behind, and it fades within a minute or two, so set up everything first and serve the food last. Food stylists often hide a wet cotton ball heated in a microwave behind the dish for more steam; never use anything unsafe near food that will be eaten. Ice cream and anything with melting cheese also need to be shot quickly.

ul: Clean the lens. Kitchens and restaurants leave oil on fingers, and an oily lens gives soft, hazy food photos.
Use 2x for 45 degree and side views. It avoids the stretched near edge you get with 1x close up.
Tap the main part of the dish to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so white plates and shiny sauces keep detail.
Turn on the grid and the level for overhead shots; the phone shows when it is flat.
Portrait mode works for food on many phones, especially side views of drinks and burgers. Check the edges of glasses and steam, which the phone often blurs wrongly.
Some phones have a food mode or scene detection that adds saturation. Check the result; it can make sauces look unreal.
Use burst for pours and drips, then pick the best frame.

sections.h: In restaurants: white balance, no flash, good manners
body: Restaurant lights are often warm and dim, so food can look orange, and a hard overhead lamp can throw a dark shadow under the plate. Before you sit down, look for a table by the window. At night, choose a seat where the main light falls on the table from the side rather than straight above. Use a white napkin or the menu as a reflector to lighten the shadow side.

If the photo looks orange, set the white balance to tungsten or a kelvin value around 3,000 to 3,500 K on a camera, or lower the warmth slightly in the phone editor. Keep a little warmth; food looks less appetizing when it is cold and blue. On a camera in dim light, start at f/1.8 to f/2.8, 1/60 to 1/125 s and ISO 800 to 3200.

body.note: Do not use flash in restaurants. It flattens the food, creates hard reflections on plates, and disturbs other diners. Take your photos quickly, do not stand on chairs, keep other guests and staff out of the frame, and follow the venue's rules; some restaurants ask guests not to take photos.

faq.q: What is the best angle for food photography?
faq.a: It depends on the shape. Flat food such as pizza or bowls looks best from overhead, most plated dishes from about 45 degrees, and tall food such as burgers, cakes and drinks from the side at table height.

faq.q: What is the best light for food photos?
faq.a: Soft daylight from a window, coming from the side or slightly behind the food. Avoid direct sun, the flash, and overhead lights straight above the plate.

faq.q: How do I make food look more appetizing in photos?
faq.a: Shoot it fresh, add garnish at the last moment, wipe the plate rim, and light it from the side so texture shows. Keep a little warmth in the color, because cool blue food looks less tasty.

faq.q: What camera settings are best for food photography?
faq.a: Start at f/2.8 to f/4 for 45 degree and side views, f/5.6 to f/8 for overhead, ISO 100 to 400, and at least 1/125 s handheld. Shoot RAW if you can so white balance is easy to fix.

faq.q: Can I use my phone for professional food photos?
faq.a: Yes. Many food photos online are taken on phones. Good window light, the 2x lens, a clean background and a steady hand matter far more than the camera.
